records.title: Heat stress on seedlings and young plants
records.summary: Bare laterite gets very hot in strong sun. Shade young plants, keep the soil covered and move watering to cool hours.
instructions: Keep mulch about a hand's depth over pits and beds so the soil stays cool.
Shade new seedlings on the afternoon side with leafy twigs, palm fronds or a propped cloth for the first couple of weeks.
Water only early morning or late afternoon, at the base, from stored water.
Sow at the start of reliable rains, when cloud and moisture protect young plants.
Plant along the shaded side of hedges, stone lines or shrubs where possible.
everyday_amounts: shade for the first couple of weeks after emergence
limitations: Shade that is too heavy or left too long makes plants weak and leggy; remove it once plants are established.
safety_notes: Work in the cool of the day; drink water and rest in shade yourself.
signs: Seedlings wilting at midday and not recovering by evening
Leaf edges scorched or bleached
Soil surface too hot to keep your palm on
Seedlings dying at the soil line on bare ground

records.title: Hot, drying wind: windbreaks and shelter
records.summary: Wind across the open plateau dries soil and seedlings fast. Build a low, partly open windbreak on the windward side and grow a living hedge.
instructions: Find the direction the drying wind usually comes from (watch dust and grass bending).
Dead hedge: pile thorny shrub prunings and dry brush into a low barrier, about knee- to waist-high, along the windward side of the plot.
Stone or brush windbreak: on very windy edges, stack stones and brush together into a low wall, leaving it partly open so wind is slowed, not forced over the top.
Live hedge: plant gliricidia cuttings or local hardy shrubs along the windward edge and along stone lines at the start of the rains.
Keep windbreaks partly open (roughly as much gap as solid): solid walls cause swirling behind them.
Weight mulch with a few stones on windy sites.
everyday_amounts: dead hedge about knee- to waist-high
a windbreak shelters a strip a few times its own height downwind
live-hedge cuttings about a pace apart
limitations: A windbreak shelters only a limited strip behind it; keep planting close to it.
Live hedges compete for water near them; keep crops a pace or so away from hedge roots.
safety_notes: Wear something on your hands when handling thorny brush.
Do not cut shrubs that hold an edge or slope in place.
signs: Soil and mulch blown away
Seedlings leaning, torn or sand-blasted
Plants drying out on one side of the plot first
Dust or loose red soil carried off on windy days

records.title: Dry spell during the wet season
records.summary: Dry gaps of a week or more are common after the first rains and mid-season. Save moisture, rescue seedlings and flowering plants first, and re-sow if needed.
instructions: Thicken mulch to about a hand's depth or more; stop any weeding that disturbs the soil.
Use stored water in this order: newly sown and seedling spots, then flowering plants, then the rest.
Give water at the base or into the mulched basin, early morning or evening; use bottle drips or a clay pot where set up.
Do not add manure or compost on top now; it will not help a dry plant.
If seedlings die, re-sow the gaps with reserved seed once soil is moist again, choosing the quickest crop if time is short.
Note the dates of the dry spell in the journal for next season's planning.
everyday_amounts: a cupful of stored water per seedling
mulch a hand's depth or more
check a finger deep under the mulch
limitations: Stored water rarely covers a long dry spell; mulch and timing do most of the work.
safety_notes: Keep drinking water separate from garden water.
signs: Leaves rolling or drooping all day and still rolled in the morning
Soil dry a finger deep under the mulch
Seedlings dying in patches
Flowers dropping

records.title: Waterlogging on flat or pooling ground
records.summary: Heavy rain can sit on top of the hard layer and drown seeds and roots. Let water out, raise planting, and keep off wet beds.
instructions: Cut an overflow notch on the downhill side of pits that hold water.
Open shallow drains, a hand deep or less, from pooling spots to a safe low point.
Raise beds or mounds higher in spots that flood; move the next sowing off the lowest ground.
Do not walk on or work wet beds; it packs the soil.
Re-sow drowned spots once the soil drains, with a crop that copes better with wet feet (finger millet or niger rather than horse gram or groundnut).
everyday_amounts: drains a hand deep or less
beds or mounds about knee-high in flood spots
limitations: Drains can start gullies if too deep or steep; keep them shallow and line with stones where they cut.
safety_notes: Never send drained water toward homes, paths or neighbours.
Stay out of moving water in storms.
signs: Water still standing in pits or around plants by the next morning
Yellowing, wilting plants in wet soil
Sour smell from the soil
Seeds rotting instead of sprouting

records.title: Heavy rain washout: repair after each storm
records.summary: Short, heavy storms wash mulch, seed and soil away. Walk the plot after every storm and repair quickly.
instructions: After each heavy rain, walk the plot once the rain stops.
Re-spread and re-firm mulch over pits and beds; pin it with a few stones.
Re-cover exposed seed and seedling roots with soil from the same pit or bed; firm gently.
Rebuild broken pit lips, basin rings and bed edges.
Close gaps in stone lines and half-moon banks; extend line ends if water went around them.
Top up washed-out beds with compost or organic matter.
Check that overflow still ends on safe ground.
everyday_amounts: a few stones to pin mulch on each pit or bed
limitations: Repeated washouts mean the catchment above is too big: add more stone lines uphill.
safety_notes: Wait until the storm and lightning have passed before going out.
signs: Mulch washed into heaps or off the plot
Seeds or seedling roots exposed
Pit rims or bed edges broken
Gaps or new channels through stone lines
Red, muddy water leaving the plot

records.title: Signs of acidity stress (unconfirmed without a lab)
records.summary: If plants grow poorly even with water and organic matter, acidic soil may be part of the reason. Respond only with gentle, reversible steps.
instructions: Add more compost or well-rotted organic matter to the pits and beds for the next sowing.
Favour tolerant crops in the next sowing: finger millet, cowpea, niger, cashew for the long term.
If you have it, the optional small handful of wood ash per pit may be tried in a few pits only, and compared with untreated pits.
Record which pits did better and expand only what works.
Do not keep adding more ash or shell: more is not better.
everyday_amounts: at most a small handful of ash per pit, in a few trial pits only
limitations: These signs also come from hunger, drought, heat or pests; acidity cannot be confirmed without a lab.
No home test, including the fizz check, measures acidity.
safety_notes: Wood ash is caustic: protect eyes and skin.
signs: Plants stay small and pale even when soil is moist and mulched
Short, stubby roots when a thinned seedling is pulled
Purplish tints on older leaves
Acid-sensitive crops failing while finger millet or cowpea nearby do better
actions: Add more compost or well-rotted organic matter to the pits and beds for the next sowing.
Favour tolerant crops in the next sowing: finger millet, cowpea, niger, cashew for the long term.

records.title: Signs of hunger (nutrient stress)
records.summary: Pale, yellowing or slow plants on poor laterite usually need more organic matter. Feed gently with compost, rotted manure and legume leaves; no recipes or fixed doses.
instructions: Work a handful or two of well-rotted compost or manure into the soil around (not touching) each plant, then re-cover with mulch.
Lay fresh gliricidia or legume leaves on beds as mulch that rots into food for the soil.
Grow cowpea or horse gram next to or after millet.
Note which pits are greener and put more organic matter in the weaker ones next season.
Avoid feeding during a dry spell; wait until the soil is moist again.
everyday_amounts: a handful or two of rotted compost or manure around each plant
an armful of fresh legume leaves per bed
limitations: Yellowing can also come from waterlogging, drought or pests; check those first.
Organic top-ups act slowly; expect changes over weeks.
safety_notes: Wash hands after handling manure; never use fresh manure on leaves you will eat.
signs: Older, lower leaves turning pale yellow first
Thin, weak stems and few tillers in millet
Small heads or few pods
Plants in pits with more compost clearly greener
